## Queues {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Queue ADT:**

- `enqueue`
- `dequeue`
- `isEmpty`

**Applications:**

- Hold jobs for a printer
- Store packets on network routers
- Make waitlists fair
- Breadth first search
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/lecture-12/penguins.png){width=62%}

::: {.ops}
```
enqueue(1)
enqueue(2)
enqueue(3)
dequeue()
dequeue()
enqueue(4)
```
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
First in, first out. The penguins go off the ice in the order they lined up.

The trace: the two dequeues return **1, then 2**. What's left, front to
back, is **3, 4**.

Compare with the stack: same three operations in spirit, but you add at one
end and remove at the *other*.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```cpp
template<class SIT>
class Queue {
public:
    // ctors dtor
    bool empty() const;
    void enqueue(const SIT & e);
    SIT dequeue();
private:
    struct queueNode {
        SIT data;
        queueNode * next;
    };
    queueNode * entry;
    queueNode * exit;
    int size;
};
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
Which pointer is `entry`, and which is `exit`?

\

What is the running time of `enqueue`?

\

What is the running time of `dequeue`?
:::
::::

::: notes
**exit** points at the front (8), **entry** at the back (4).

- `enqueue` adds after the back node and moves `entry`: $\Theta(1)$.
- `dequeue` removes the front node and moves `exit`: $\Theta(1)$.

Ask what happens if they are the other way round. Adding at the front is
fine, but removing from the back of a *singly* linked list means walking to
the node before it: $\Theta(n)$. So the direction of the arrows decides which
end is which.
:::

## Queue — array based implementation: {.smaller .smallcode}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
```cpp
template<class SIT>
class Queue {
public:
    // ctors dtor
    bool empty() const;
    void enqueue(const SIT & e);
    SIT dequeue();
private:
    vector<SIT> items;
};
```

```
enqueue(4);       enqueue(3);

enqueue(7);       dequeue();
dequeue();        enqueue(9);
dequeue();
```

::::

::: notes
Trace it with two indices, front and back, instead of shifting anything.

After the first column the queue is just **7**, sitting at index 3. After
`enqueue` 2, 1, 3, 5 it fills indices 3–7: the end of the array. One more
`dequeue` leaves **2 1 3 5** in indices 4–7.

Now `enqueue(9)`: there's no room at the end, but indices 0–3 are empty.
Shifting everything left would cost $\Theta(n)$ per `dequeue`. The better
idea: wrap around and put 9 at index 0. That's the next slide.
:::

::: notes
The blank lines in `private:` are for the class to fill in: **`int exit;`**
and **`int size;`**. The back of the queue isn't stored — it's
`(exit + size) % capacity`.

Trace: m o n d a y fill 4–7 and wrap to 0–1; i s fill 2–3. The array is
full: **m o n d a y i s**. `dequeue` returns **m** and moves exit to 5.
`enqueue(h)` goes in the slot m left, index 4. Now `enqueue(a)` finds it full
again, so resize: copy into the long array **in queue order, starting at
exit** — o n d a y i s h — and then add a. Exit becomes 0.

Same doubling as Friday's video, so both operations are $\Theta(1)$ on
average.
:::

## Summary: {.smaller}

**Linked list based implementation of a stack:**

Constant time `push` and `pop`.

\

**Array based implementation of a stack:**

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ time `pop`.

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ time `push` if capacity exists.

Cost over $O(n)$ pushes is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ for an AVERAGE of \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ per push.

\

**Why consider an array?**

::: notes
Blanks: **constant**, **constant**, **$O(n)$**, **$O(1)$**. That last pair
is Nathan's resizing video in one line: doubling makes the total cost of $n$
pushes linear, so each push is constant on average.

Why an array at all: no pointer stored with every item, so less memory; the
items sit next to each other, so the cache helps; and you can index into the
middle in constant time. The queue gets all the same answers.
:::

Running time?

::: notes
The blank: an array **whose two halves are each sorted**.

Walk two fingers, one at the start of each half. Copy the smaller of the
two into the output and advance that finger. When one half runs out, copy
the rest of the other.

Every element is copied exactly once, so this is **merge**, and it is
$\Theta(n)$.
:::

::: notes
Split it in half. *If* each half were sorted, one merge would finish the
job in linear time.

So how did the halves get sorted? Leave them hanging: that's merge sort, in
Friday's video.
:::

## mergeSort {.smaller .smallcode}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
1. If the array has 0 or 1 elements, it's sorted.
2. Split the array into halves.
3. Sort each half recursively.
4. Merge the two halves.
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```cpp
void mergeSort(vector<T> & A, int lo, int hi) {
    if (hi > lo) {
        int mid = (hi + lo)/2;
        mergeSort(A, lo, mid);
        mergeSort(A, mid+1, hi);
        merge(A, lo, mid, hi);
    }
}
```
:::
